abstract: Memory-native evolution requires making memory an intrinsic capability of foundation models, enabling them to continuously accumulate and utilize information. To this end, we introduce MemT-1.0, a new architecture of memory foundation models that internalize memory as part of model computation. Building on Metis, MemT-1.0 employs Gated DeltaNet-2 with a stable token-level memory update mechanism within each turn. We further introduce Mixture-of-Storage to scale native memory capacity. Following a deliberate backbone preparation, we develop a two-stage training pipeline consisting of continued pre-training and post-training, supported by 34B tokens of training data and efficient training and inference infrastructure. We release a model family comprising MemT-1.0-Nano and MemT-1.0-Flash, and conduct a comprehensive evaluation of memory and general capabilities. The results show that they outperform the parametric memory baselines on average and remain competitive with retrieval-augmented methods, while largely preserving general capabilities. At a history length of 128K tokens, MemT-1.0-Nano achieves approximately $1.86\times$ end-to-end inference speedup and a $66\times$ reduction in persistent storage relative to full context KV cache. By internalizing retrieved procedural experience, MemT-1.0 improves task success on agentic tasks, providing a practical step toward memory-native evolution.

sections.body: The paper introduces MemT-1.0, which keeps the dynamic local memory and trainable hyper memory from Metis and replaces token selection with a token-level update based on Gated DeltaNet-2 (GDN-2). Mixture-of-Storage (MoS) scales native memory capacity. The release comprises MemT-1.0-Nano (36B parameters, 3B activated, 10M dynamic memory) and MemT-1.0-Flash (288B parameters, 17B activated, 336M dynamic memory). Training uses 34B tokens in two stages. Across 11 memory benchmarks, the models outperform parametric memory baselines on average. On SWE-bench Verified and SWE-bench Multilingual, procedural experience internalized into native memory improves average task success over agents without experience.
sections.heading: Introduction
sections.headline: MemT-1.0 upgrades the Metis memory design and releases 36B and 288B parameter models with Mixture-of-Storage.

sections.body: MemT-1.0 augments selected Transformer blocks with a native memory block. For each such block, the original attention output and a memory attention output are summed, and the backbone's pre-attention, attention and post-attention operations are kept unchanged. The dynamic memory state is a multi-channel matrix per layer, initialized to zero for each new trajectory and updated across steps. The hyper memory block holds the memory query, key and value projections and the gating parameters, which are optimized during training and fixed during online interaction. Mixture-of-Storage (MoS) gives each memory block several parallel experts, each with its own storage and utilization routing. The Nano model uses Qwen3.6-35B-A3B as backbone, and the Flash model uses a post-trained DeepSeek-V4-Flash.
sections.heading: Model Architecture
sections.headline: Native memory runs as a parallel attention branch in selected Transformer blocks, with backbone layers left unchanged.

sections.body: The backbone is first post-trained on 126.5K trajectories (2.4B tokens), which improves all six monitored benchmarks by 6.3 points on average over the public release. Tasks the backbone never solves stay near 1.6 to 4.0% accuracy, while supplying the relevant facts in context raises accuracy on a probe set from 27% to 91%, so the authors treat new information as what native memory must supply. Memory training then uses 20B tokens of continued pre-training data and 14B tokens of post-training data. Only memory parameters are optimized. The loss is a forward KL divergence from the frozen backbone teacher's top-64 token distribution, with the student evaluated under teacher forcing.
sections.heading: Training
sections.headline: Backbone preparation and a two-stage pipeline train memory by distilling from a frozen full-context teacher on 34B tokens.

sections.body: Training packs keep attention within each step and let memory carry state between steps of the same trajectory, while the backbone runs layer by layer. Memory updates are chunked, and all queries in a step read the same incoming state. For Mixture-of-Storage, windowed execution projects one group of complete steps at a time and recomputes intermediates during backward. In Table 1, a 2048-token window cuts peak memory by 87.4% and raises forward-backward time by 6.6%. At inference, the per-trajectory state size is fixed by the memory configuration, so persistent storage does not grow with the number of interactions. Shared weights and active key-value caches are excluded from this measurement.
sections.heading: System and Infrastructure
sections.headline: Windowed execution of Mixture-of-Storage cuts peak memory by 80.1% for a 32K-token pack, adding 1.6% to forward-backward time.

sections.body: Scaling is studied on MemT-1.0-Nano along two axes: continued post-training exposure over two epochs of the same corpus, and the number of Mixture-of-Storage experts. Across sampled checkpoints, the average score moves from 36.65 to 46.80 with intermediate fluctuations. Most of the early gain arrives within the first quarter epoch, and LoCoMo rises from 40.39 to 55.39 across the first epoch. After 400 CPT steps, four experts gain 0.41 points on average at 200 post-training steps, and gain 2.01 and 2.69 points at 3,400 and 5,500 steps. The authors state these results suggest remaining room for optimization at fixed memory capacity.
sections.heading: Memory Scaling Behavior
sections.headline: Memory score rises from 36.65 to 46.80 over two post-training epochs, and four experts beat two by up to 2.69 points.

sections.body: Both models are evaluated on 11 memory benchmarks without historical text in the query, with answers scored by a gpt-4.1-mini judge. MemT-1.0-Flash and MemT-1.0-Nano rank first and second among parametric methods, ahead of the strongest parametric baseline by 12.5 and 8.9 points. Textual memory systems still score substantially higher on LongMemEval-S and BEAM-1M. Under the noise setting, Flash performs comparably to its backbone on average, and Nano's average decrease is around one point, concentrated on LiveCodeBench v6. At a history length of 128K tokens, Nano's per-trajectory storage is 66× smaller than full context. Low-rank truncation of the memory state shows that returns diminish as retained rank increases.
sections.heading: Evaluation
sections.headline: Native memory averages 50.6 on memory benchmarks for Flash and 47.0 for Nano, ahead of parametric baselines but behind textual systems.

sections.body: The authors build an experience bank of 1,040 coding experiences from 41,057 successful trajectories, then construct 42,403 training samples through counterfactual interventions at breakpoints in failed trajectories. MemT-1.0-Nano is post-trained with the backbone frozen, optimizing only the hyper memory, using distillation with full-suffix supervision. On SWE-bench Verified in the Before Execution setting, average success is 69.33% against 66.07% without experience and 68.87% with textual experience. The pass^3 measure rises from 54.00% to 61.60%, matching textual experience. The authors note that the framework relies on externally constructed experience, and that storing experience adds computation.
sections.heading: Application in Agentic Tasks
sections.headline: Stored procedural experience raises the coding benchmark success rate from 66.07% to 69.33% without experience text in context.

sections.body: The memory state is O(1) with respect to interaction history length N, so it cannot keep detailed history the way methods whose stored representations grow as O(N) can. Each update folds new information into an existing representation, which creates trade-offs between keeping earlier details and adding recent ones. The authors state that this loss of memory fidelity remains a challenge for tasks that require precise recall. They also suggest the recurrent organization could support successive compression of experience. Open questions include whether experience in local memory can be consolidated into hyper memory parameters through further training, and how hyper memory can be adapted through local memory.
sections.heading: Limitations and Discussion
sections.headline: A fixed-size memory state limits recall of detail, and the relation between local and hyper memory remains unresolved.

sections.body: The conclusion states that both MemT-1.0 models outperform the evaluated parametric memory baselines on average while largely preserving the general capabilities of their backbones under the noise setting. The main components named are token-level stable memory updates, Mixture-of-Storage, backbone preparation, and the two-stage training pipeline. Coding-agent results are cited as evidence that native memory can internalize procedural experience to improve task success and execution consistency. Future work is listed as improving long-term memory, scaling memory capacity, reducing the cost of memory updates, and exploring autonomous experience acquisition and continual memory consolidation.
sections.heading: Conclusion
sections.headline: MemT-1.0 outperforms the evaluated parametric baselines on average, preserves general capabilities under noise, and points to future memory scaling.

sections.body: Appendix A lists contributors and acknowledgments. Appendix B gives Table 6 with the memory geometry of both models, including 450,931,360 trainable memory parameters for Nano and 3,608,608,000 for Flash, and Table 7 with execution and distillation settings. It describes how memory projections are initialized from backbone attention projections, and how gates and forget-gate time scales are initialized. Appendix C derives a bound for a recursive update: when the propagation norm is below one, the state norm is bounded by R divided by one minus rho. The appendix also contains worked examples of memory abstention, rule application and tracking an update, and details of the experience data construction.
sections.heading: Appendix
sections.headline: The appendix gives author lists, memory configurations, projection and gate initialization, training settings, and a stability bound for the update.
